hints: Think about what white solid gives $CO_2$ with dilute $HNO_3$. That gas turns limewater milky, so link this to the familiar carbonate residue from Group 1 decomposition.
walkthrough:
Work out what the residue must be**
You are told the white residue fizzes with $HNO_3(aq)$ to give a gas that turns limewater milky. That is the classic test for $CO_2$, and it tells you the solid contains carbonate. For lithium, the residue is $\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3$.

Balance the atoms that are left over**
Start with $\text{Li}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O}$. If $\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3$ keeps one C and three O atoms, you still have one C, one O from the oxalate plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to account for. That fits perfectly as $\text{CO}$ plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, both gases on gentle heating. So the full equation is $\text{Li}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}$.

hints: Recall the trend in Group 2 nitrates and carbonates. The less stable salt is always the one with the smaller, more polarising cation.
Compare $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ in size and think about how the cation distorts the large $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ anion to help it break apart.
walkthrough:
Picture the cation pulling on the anion**
Think of the $2+$ ion sitting next to the large $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ ion. A very small, concentrated positive charge pulls electron density out of the anion and distorts it. That distortion weakens the C-C and C-O bonds inside the anion, so less heat is needed to break it up.

Compare calcium with barium**
$\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ with the same $2+$ charge, so $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ has the higher charge density and greater polarising power. It distorts $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ more strongly, making $\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4$ less thermally stable. Therefore $\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4$ decomposes at the lower temperature, exactly as for Group 2 nitrates.

Final answer: $\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4$ decomposes at the lower temperature.
$\text{Ca}^{2+}$ has a smaller ionic radius / higher charge density than $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, so it polarises / distorts the $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ anion more, weakening bonds within the anion.

hints: Remember that in a free metal ion the five d orbitals have the same energy, but ligands approaching along different axes change that.
Think about what happens when an electron absorbs exactly the right amount of light energy to move between those split levels.
Connect the colour you absorb to the colour you see. The solution shows the light that is not absorbed.
walkthrough:
See why the d orbitals are no longer equal**
In $\text{[Fe(C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}$ the $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is surrounded octahedrally by oxalate oxygens. Lone pairs on the ligands repel d electrons differently depending on orbital orientation, so the five d orbitals split into two sets of different energy. This is called d-d splitting.

Follow the electron jump**
$\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is $3d^5$, so there are vacancies in the upper set. An electron in a lower d orbital can absorb a photon with energy $\Delta E = h\nu$ exactly equal to the gap and jump up. That is a d-d transition.

Link absorption to green**
Only certain wavelengths are absorbed, in this case mainly red light. What passes through to your eyes is everything else. Your brain perceives the mixture of the remaining transmitted wavelengths as the complementary colour, here green.

Final answer: Ligands cause the d orbitals to split into orbitals of different energy.
Electrons are promoted / excited from a lower to a higher d orbital by absorbing light energy.
The colour observed is the complementary colour to the light absorbed.

hints: Count K and Fe first. The products contain $2 + 2 = 4$ K per Fe unit in a way that needs doubling of the reactant to balance.
walkthrough:
Balance metals before ligands**
Look at K and Fe. Left side has $\text{K}_3\text{Fe}$ per formula. Right side has $\text{K}_2\text{Fe}$ in the iron(II) complex plus $\text{K}_2$ in potassium ethanedioate. Doubling the iron complex to $2\text{K}_3\text{Fe(C}_2\text{O}_4)_3$ gives $6$ K and $2$ Fe, which matches $2 \times \text{K}_2\text{Fe(C}_2\text{O}_4)_2$ plus one $\text{K}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$.

Check oxalate and carbon dioxide**
Left side now has $6$ $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$ groups. Right side uses $4$ in the two iron(II) complexes plus $1$ in $\text{K}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$, leaving one $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$ equivalent which appears as $2\text{CO}_2$. The balanced equation is $2\text{K}_3\text{Fe(C}_2\text{O}_4)_3 \rightarrow 2\text{K}_2\text{Fe(C}_2\text{O}_4)_2 + \text{K}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 + 2\text{CO}_2$.
Final answer: $2\text{K}_3\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3 \rightarrow 2\text{K}_2\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_2 + \text{K}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 + 2\text{CO}_2$

hints: Picture Fe at the centre of an octahedron with three $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ chelate rings. There is no plane of symmetry, so expect a chiral propeller shape.
Think of left-handed and right-handed propellers. The two isomers are mirror images that need opposite arrangements of the three O-O arcs around the vertical Fe axis.
walkthrough:
Build the octahedral propeller**
Each $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ is bidentate, drawn as $\text{O} \cap \text{O}$, occupying two adjacent octahedral positions. With three such chelates you fill all six positions around $\text{Fe}$. Viewed down an axis the three rings look like the blades of a propeller twisting one way.

Draw the mirror image pair**
For isomer 1, draw one O of each chelate above the plane with a wedge and one below with a hatch, all twisting clockwise. For isomer 2, reverse the twist to anticlockwise so every wedge becomes a hatch in the mirror. The two 3D sketches are optical isomers, they are mirror images that cannot be superimposed.

Final answer: Two three-dimensional octahedral structures each with Fe at centre and three bidentate $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ ligands shown as O-O chelates.
Isomer 1 shows one propeller arrangement (e.g. delta) and isomer 2 shows the mirror image propeller arrangement (e.g. lambda), non-superimposable, with wedges / solid lines for bonds out of plane and hatched lines for bonds into plane.

hints: Recall that a buffer removes added $\text{H}^+$ by turning it into a weak acid. Here $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-$ can accept a proton.
Recall that a buffer removes added $\text{OH}^-$ by donating a proton to make water, leaving the conjugate base $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$.
walkthrough:
Deal with added acid**
$\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-$ can act as a base. When a little strong acid is added, it mops up $\text{H}^+$ to form the weak acid $\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$: $$\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$$ Because the added $\text{H}^+$ is locked up, $\text{[H}^+]$ hardly changes.

Deal with added alkali**
$\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-$ can also act as an acid. When a little $\text{OH}^-$ is added, it donates its proton: $$\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^- + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ The added $\text{OH}^-$ is converted to water, so pH stays almost constant.

Final answer: $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$
$\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^- + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Identify which half-equation runs as reduction ($\text{O}_2$ to $\text{OH}^-$) and which must be reversed as oxidation ($\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ to $\text{CO}_2$), then balance electrons.
Remember $E^\ominus_{cell} = E^\ominus_{cathode} - E^\ominus_{anode}$ using the reduction potentials as given, without multiplying the $E^\ominus$ values.
walkthrough:
Combine the half-equations**
The more positive $E^\ominus$ is the cathode: $$\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) + 4e^- \rightleftharpoons 4\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$$ The oxalate couple is the anode and must be reversed to oxidation: $$\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + 2e^-$$ Multiply the oxidation by 2 to give $4e^-$ and add to cancel electrons: $$2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + \text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) \rightarrow 4\text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$$

Calculate the standard cell potential**
Use reduction potentials directly: $$E^\ominus_{cell} = E^\ominus_{cathode} - E^\ominus_{anode}$$ $$E^\ominus_{cell} = +0.40 - (-0.59) = +0.99\ \text{V}$$ The positive value shows the oxidation of ethanedioate by oxygen is feasible in the fuel cell.

Final answer: overall cell reaction: $2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + \text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) \rightarrow 4\text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$
$E^\ominus_{cell} = +0.99\ \text{V}$
